items.q: A 52-year-old woman with an intact uterus presents with debilitating hot flushes, night sweats, and sleep disturbances occurring multiple times daily for 6 months. Her last menstrual period was 14 months ago. She has no personal or family history of breast cancer or thromboembolism. Which HRT regimen is most appropriate?
o: Continuous combined oral or transdermal estrogen plus progestogen
Unopposed oral conjugated equine estrogen monotherapy
Cyclic sequential estrogen plus progestogen with monthly withdrawal bleeds
items.exp: In a postmenopausal woman (> 12 months amenorrhoea) with an intact uterus, continuous combined estrogen plus progestogen therapy is the regimen of choice. The addition of daily progestogen prevents unopposed estrogen-induced endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, while continuous administration achieves endometrial atrophy and amenorrhoea.
r: Correct. Continuous combined HRT controls vasomotor symptoms and protects the intact endometrium while maintaining amenorrhoea.
Incorrect. Unopposed estrogen in a woman with an intact uterus dramatically increases endometrial adenocarcinoma risk.
Incorrect. Cyclic sequential regimens are used in perimenopause when preserving withdrawal bleeds; postmenopausal women prefer amenorrhoea.
Incorrect. Progestin monotherapy is second-line, less effective for vasomotor symptoms and causes mood side effects.
items.kp: Postmenopausal women with an intact uterus require continuous combined estrogen plus progestogen to prevent endometrial cancer.

items.q: Why is transdermal 17-beta estradiol preferred over oral estrogen formulations in women requiring HRT who have a body mass index of 33 kg/m² or hypertension?
o: It bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism and does not increase venous thromboembolism risk
It has higher binding affinity for bone estrogen receptors
It does not require concurrent progestogen in women with an intact uterus
It completely eliminates the risk of breast cancer
items.exp: Oral estrogens undergo first-pass hepatic metabolism, inducing hepatic synthesis of procoagulant clotting factors (VII, VIII, IX, prothrombin) and sex hormone-binding globulin, significantly increasing venous thromboembolism (VTE) and stroke risk. Transdermal estradiol bypasses the portal circulation, demonstrating neutral VTE risk in observational and randomized trials.
r: Correct. Transdermal estrogen avoids hepatic first-pass activation and carries no increased VTE risk.
Incorrect. Binding affinity for bone receptors is identical between oral and transdermal formulations.
Incorrect. Transdermal estrogen still stimulates the endometrium and mandates progestogen if uterus is present.
Incorrect. It does not eliminate breast cancer risk associated with long-term combined therapy.
items.kp: Transdermal estrogen avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism and does not increase the risk of venous thromboembolism.

items.q: A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with severe vaginal dryness, burning, and dyspareunia. She has no hot flushes, night sweats, or systemic climacteric complaints. Physical examination confirms pale, thinned, dry vaginal mucosa with loss of rugae. What is the treatment of choice?
items.exp: For isolated genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM / atrophic vaginitis) without systemic vasomotor symptoms, low-dose local vaginal estrogen (cream, tablet, or ring) is the first-line treatment of choice. Systemic absorption is minimal, so concurrent progestogen is not required even in women with an intact uterus.
r: Correct. Low-dose local vaginal estrogen treats GSM effectively without significant systemic absorption or progestin need.
Incorrect. Systemic HRT exposes the patient to unnecessary systemic risks when complaints are strictly local.
Incorrect. Systemic transdermal estrogen requires progestogen and carries systemic exposure.
Incorrect. Oral SERMs are second-line to topical local therapy.
items.kp: Low-dose local topical vaginal estrogen is first-line for genitourinary syndrome of menopause and does not require progestogen.

items.q: Which of the following conditions represents an absolute contraindication to systemic hormone replacement therapy?
o: Active or past history of breast cancer
items.exp: Absolute contraindications to systemic HRT include: active, recent, or past history of breast cancer; active estrogen-sensitive malignant neoplasms (endometrial cancer); unexplained abnormal vaginal bleeding; active deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism; active liver disease; and recent myocardial infarction or stroke.
r: Correct. Personal history of breast cancer is an absolute contraindication to systemic HRT.
Incorrect. Controlled hypertension is a precaution where transdermal HRT is safe and preferred.
Incorrect. Well-controlled diabetes is not a contraindication; transdermal estrogen has neutral glycemic effects.
Incorrect. Osteopenia/osteoporosis is an indication for bone protection with HRT.
items.kp: A personal history of breast cancer, active VTE, or undiagnosed vaginal bleeding are absolute contraindications to systemic HRT.

items.q: What neuroendocrine alteration is directly responsible for triggering the acute sensation of hot flushes in menopausal women?
o: Hypertrophy of hypothalamic KNDy (kisspeptin, neurokinin B, dynorphin) neurons narrowing the thermoneutral zone
Excessive release of melatonin from the pineal gland
Direct peripheral alpha-1 adrenergic constriction of skin vessels
Downregulation of thyroid-stimulating hormone receptors in brown fat
items.exp: Estrogen withdrawal causes loss of negative feedback on hypothalamic KNDy neurons (kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin) located in the arcuate nucleus. These hypertrophied neurons project to the thermoregulatory center in the preoptic area, dramatically narrowing the body's thermoneutral zone so minor temperature shifts trigger massive heat-dissipation responses (vasodilation and sweating).
r: Correct. Estrogen deficiency unleashes hypothalamic KNDy neurons, narrowing the thermoregulatory set-point.
Incorrect. Melatonin regulates circadian sleep rhythms, not vasomotor flush cascades.
Incorrect. Vasomotor flushes involve cutaneous vasodilation, not constriction.
Incorrect. Thyroid receptors in brown fat mediate non-shivering thermogenesis, not episodic flushes.
items.kp: Menopausal hot flushes stem from hypothalamic KNDy neuron activation narrowing the preoptic thermoneutral zone.

items.q: Which non-hormonal, selective neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptor antagonist was recently approved for the treatment of moderate-to-severe menopausal vasomotor symptoms in women with contraindications to estrogen?
items.exp: Fezolinetant is a novel, non-hormonal, highly selective neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptor antagonist that directly blocks neurokinin B signaling on hypertrophied KNDy neurons in the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center, restoring normal thermoregulation without estrogenic stimulation. It is FDA/EMA approved for menopausal vasomotor symptoms.
r: Correct. Fezolinetant is a targeted NK3 receptor antagonist approved for non-hormonal management of vasomotor flushes.
Incorrect. Paroxetine is an SSRI with modest off-label flush reduction.
Incorrect. Gabapentin is an anticonvulsant used off-label.
Incorrect. Clonidine is a centrally acting alpha-2 agonist with modest efficacy and high side effects.
items.kp: Fezolinetant is a non-hormonal selective NK3 receptor antagonist that blocks hypothalamic KNDy signaling to treat hot flushes.

items.q: In the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) randomized trial, which adverse outcome demonstrated a statistically significant increase in the estrogen-plus-progestin arm compared to placebo after 5 years of use?
items.exp: The WHI combined continuous estrogen plus progestin arm demonstrated a statistically significant increase in invasive breast cancer (HR 1.24), coronary heart disease, stroke, and pulmonary embolism. In contrast, it demonstrated significant reductions in osteoporotic hip fractures and colorectal cancer.
r: Correct. The WHI trial demonstrated an increased risk of invasive breast cancer with combined continuous estrogen and progestin.
Incorrect. Colorectal cancer incidence was actually reduced by 37% in the combined HRT arm.
Incorrect. Osteoporotic hip fractures were significantly reduced by 34%.
Incorrect. Endometrial cancer was not increased due to the protective progestin component.
items.kp: Long-term combined continuous HRT in the WHI trial was associated with a small increased risk of invasive breast cancer and thromboembolism.

items.q: A 49-year-old woman with a prior total abdominal hysterectomy for uterine fibroids 4 years ago presents with severe menopausal hot flushes and night sweats. Which HRT regimen is indicated?
items.exp: Women who have undergone total hysterectomy have no endometrium and therefore do not require progestogen for endometrial protection. They should be prescribed estrogen-only therapy. In fact, the WHI estrogen-alone arm (in hysterectomized women) showed no increased risk of breast cancer over 7 years of use.
r: Correct. Estrogen-only therapy is standard for hysterectomized women, as progestogen is only needed for endometrial protection.
Incorrect. Progestogen is unnecessary without a uterus and contributes to adverse breast and vascular profiles.
Incorrect. Progestogen monotherapy is ineffective and unnecessary.
Incorrect. Raloxifene is an anti-estrogen in breast and brain, worsening hot flushes.
items.kp: Hysterectomized women should receive estrogen-only therapy; progestogen is not required and should be avoided.

items.q: What is the recognized 'window of opportunity' (timing hypothesis) for initiating systemic HRT to maximize cardiovascular benefits and minimize vascular risks?
o: Initiation within 10 years of menopause onset and age under 60 years
Initiation at least 15 years after menopause onset
Initiation only after confirmation of coronary calcification
items.exp: The 'timing hypothesis' established that initiating systemic HRT in the 'window of opportunity'—within 10 years of menopause onset or before age 60—demonstrates cardiovascular benefits, reduced all-cause mortality, and minimal adverse vascular events. Initiating HRT > 10 years post-menopause or after age 60 increases coronary and stroke risks due to pre-existing atherosclerotic plaque destabilization.
r: Correct. HRT initiation within 10 years of menopause and under age 60 carries the most favorable risk-benefit profile.
Incorrect. Initiating > 10-15 years postmenopause increases cardiovascular events.
Incorrect. Starting after age 70 carries substantial thrombotic and stroke risks.
Incorrect. Pre-existing calcification indicates advanced plaque vulnerable to estrogen-induced disruption.
items.kp: The window of opportunity for HRT is within 10 years of menopause onset and age under 60 years.

items.q: Which selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) has estrogen-agonist activity on bone and cardiovascular lipids, but estrogen-antagonist activity on breast and endometrium, making it useful for postmenopausal osteoporosis prevention without endometrial stimulation?
items.exp: Raloxifene is a second-generation SERM that acts as an estrogen agonist on bone (preventing postmenopausal bone loss and vertebral fractures) and lipid metabolism, while exerting strong antagonistic effects on breast tissue (reducing ER-positive breast cancer risk) and the endometrium (does not cause endometrial hyperplasia or bleeding).
r: Correct. Raloxifene protects bone and breast while remaining neutral/antagonistic on the endometrium.
Incorrect. Tamoxifen is an agonist on the endometrium, increasing endometrial polyp, hyperplasia, and cancer risks.
Incorrect. Clomiphene is primarily an ovulatory induction agent.
Incorrect. Letrozole is an aromatase inhibitor, which induces bone loss rather than protecting it.
items.kp: Raloxifene acts as an estrogen agonist on bone while antagonizing breast and endometrial tissues.
